newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portugal rejects EU olive subsidy plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portugal rejects EU olive subsidy plan.

text.p: Portugal said on Monday it rejected a European Union plan to reform subsidies for olive farmers because the proposal would destroy production.

Portugal also said it sought to boost olive production as the industry had strong potential to provide incomes to farmers hit by desertification and to satisfy demand by domestic consumers and export markets.
The European Commission offers subsidies based on production rates, but has proposed switching this to a system based on the number of olive trees, to clamp down on fraud.
Portuguese Agriculture Minister Fernando Gomes da Silva said under such a proposal farmers receiving subsidies based on the number of trees on their land would have no incentive to produce olives.

"We don't want policy measures that contribute to the destruction of production," he told Reuters on the sidelines of a four-day conference of the International Olive Oil Council (IOC) in Lisbon, which began on Monday.
"The problem is that we need measures that support production and give incentives to develop production," he added.
Earlier, the minister told the conference "I hope that the IOC sends a statement to the European Union's Agriculture Commissioner opposing reform based on the number of trees."
More than 50,000 Spaniards protested in Madrid on Saturday against the EU reform proposal.

Spain says the new plan would cut vital subsidies to as low as 30 billion pesetas ($207.7 million) from around 100 billion now, crippling an industry that provides thousands of jobs in some of the economically weakest parts of the nation.
Olive oil prices have been falling sharply since last September. The IOC has estimated output could surge by 38 percent in 1996/97 from 1995/96, and prices will fall further this year.
Gomes da Silva said he expected the European Commission to take a final decision on whether to implement reforms by late summer.

Fausto Luchetti, executive director of the IOC, told Reuters: "If you give an amount per tree, regardless what happens with the cultivation of the tree, that surely is a disincentive for olive oil production. That would be the worst system to replace the present one."
He added: "You have to look at the nuances in the measures. But I am confident that the Commission and the present member states will together find a solution."
The IOC represents 24 countries responsible for 93 percent of the world's olive oil production. The EU accounts for about 70 percent of global production.
Gomes da Silva said Portugal would treat the olive oil industry as a priority as it could provide a living to farmers in areas hit by desertification.

"The need to provide incomes to farmers in the most economically depressed and parched areas, the absence of alternative crops and the needs for domestic consumption and to provide exports, make this sector a priority area," he said.
Growing markets in North America, Asia and northern Europe could absorb the glut in olive oil production, officials said.

Asked to comment on the impact of falling olive oil prices for the industry, Luchetti said: "I don't think this is bad news," adding: "We are dealing with expansion of consumption in South East Asia, Japan, and in America."
Luchetti said it was vital to inform consumers around the world that olive oil was a healthy product so that demand would increase.
Gomes da Silva said: "The prospects of world markets, namely in northern Europe, Asia and America, clearly encourage increased production."
